title: 第十六章 城门口
content_zh:
云中城的城墙，是江砚长这么大见过最高的东西。

    不是沈家村那种夯土院墙，一脚能踹出个坑。是真正的城墙，青灰的大砖一层压一层，往上垒到他得仰着脖子、脖子都酸了才看得见垛口。墙根底下熏得发黑，一道道水渍往下淌，像谁哭花了脸。墙头插着几杆破旗，被北风刮得啪啪响，旗面早褪成了灰白，看不出原先是什么颜色。

    江砚混在一拨进城的流民里头，慢慢往城门挪。

    他这两天是怎么熬过来的，自己也记不真切了。雪夜里逃出沈家村，先是没命地跑，跑到腿软了就爬，爬到爬不动了，就缩在一个废弃的窝棚里抖。那柄从绳索上割下来的铁片刀，他贴身揣着，凉冰冰地硌着胸口，可他不敢扔——那是他眼下唯一能攥住的、证明那桩“邪门事“真发生过的东西。

    呕过血之后，他整个人像被抽掉了一层筋。走两步喘三步，眼前时不时发黑。他啃过路边冻硬的草根，喝过化开的雪水，靠着一股说不清的劲，一路往云中城摸。

    为什么是云中城？

    因为原主脑子里，关于这座城的记忆最多。镇上人提起它，总说“城里乱归乱，到底是大城，能讨口饭吃“。江砚没别的去处，逃奴的罪名压在背上，他只能往人多的地方钻——人越多，越没人盯着他这么一个面黄肌瘦的小子。

    城门口排着长队。

    要进城，得交“门税“。

    江砚原先不知道这一茬，是排在前头一个挑担的老汉小声告诉他的。两个守城的兵卒，一个坐在小马扎上嗑瓜子，一个挎着腰刀来回踱，谁要进城，先伸手。

    “进城，半个钱。“踱步那个兵卒嗓门粗，“挑担的，担子上有货的，再加。“

    队伍往前蹭。

    轮到江砚前头那个挑担老汉，老汉佝着腰，从怀里掏出个布包，一层层解开，捏出两枚磨得发亮的铜钱，递过去。

    “就这点？“兵卒不接，眼一斜，瞟向老汉担子里那几捆干柴，“你这柴，城里能卖几个钱，你心里没数？“

    “军爷……“老汉的腰又弯了几分，“这柴是给城里王老爷家送的，早讲好了价，小老儿就挣个脚力钱……“

    “王老爷？“兵卒嗤笑一声，“哪个王老爷，啊？我怎么不认得？“他用刀鞘挑了挑那柴捆，“我看你这是私贩。私贩，扣了。“

    老汉急了：“军爷！军爷不能啊！这要扣了，小老儿这趟白跑，回去没法交代——”

    “滚一边去。”兵卒不耐烦地一推。

    老汉一个趔趄，担子歪了，柴捆散落一地。他扑过去捡，被那兵卒一脚踩住一捆，慢条斯理道：“想拿走，行。把你怀里那布包，留下。”

    江砚站在后头，看着。

    他心里那股子又熟悉、又冰冷的东西，慢慢往上涌。

    跟沈家村，跟那管事，跟江狗剩，没什么两样。换了身皮，换了个地方，欺负人的法子，竟是一模一样。强的，欺弱的；弱的，再去欺更弱的。这世道，从村里到城里，根子上是一样的烂。

    排队的人没一个吭声。

    一个抱孩子的妇人低着头，一个赶驴的汉子把脸别向一边，几个流民缩着脖子盯着自己的脚尖。谁都看见了，谁都不看。

    江砚也低下了头。

    他不是不想说话。他是知道，自己这会儿说一个字，都可能把自己搭进去。逃奴，没钱，一身的伤——他比那老汉还不如。

    老汉终究是把那布包留下了，捡起几捆零散的柴，挑着空了大半的担子，一声不吭地进了城。走过江砚身边时，江砚看见他眼眶是红的，可没掉泪——许是这种事，他经得多了，泪早干了。

    轮到江砚。
content_en:
The city wall of Yunzhong City is the tallest thing Jiang Yan has ever seen.

    It's not a rammed earth courtyard wall like the one in Shenjia Village, where you can make a hole with just one kick. It was a real city wall, with large green and gray bricks laid one on top of the other, so high that he had to tilt his head back and his neck was sore to see the crenellations. The bottom of the wall was blackened with smoke, and water stains were dripping down, looking like someone was crying. There were several broken flags stuck on the wall, which were blown by the north wind. The flags had long since faded to gray and it was hard to tell what their original color was.

    Jiang Yan mingled with a group of refugees entering the city and slowly moved towards the city gate.

    How he survived the past two days, he couldn't remember exactly. I escaped from Shenjia Village on a snowy night. I ran desperately at first, then crawled when my legs became weak. When I couldn't crawl anymore, I huddled in an abandoned shack and shivered. He held the iron knife cut from the rope close to his body, feeling cold against his chest, but he did not dare to throw it away - it was the only thing he could hold on to prove that the "evil thing" really happened.

    After vomiting blood, his whole body looked like a layer of muscles had been ripped out. After taking two steps and taking a breath for three steps, my vision would turn black from time to time. He gnawed on the frozen grass roots on the roadside, drank the melted snow water, and relied on an indescribable energy to touch all the way to Yunzhong City.

    Why Cloud City?

    Because the original owner has the most memories of this city in his mind. When people in the town mention it, they always say, "Chaos in the city will lead to chaos. After all, it is a big city and you can make a living." Jiang Yan had no other place to go, and with the charge of being a runaway slave weighing on his back, he had no choice but to sneak into a place with a lot of people - the more people there were, the fewer people would stare at a skinny boy like him.

    There was a long queue at the city gate.

    To enter the city, you have to pay a "gate tax."

    Jiang Yan didn't know about this at first, but an old man in front of him whispered to him. Two soldiers guarding the city, one was sitting on a pony eating melon seeds, and the other was pacing back and forth with a waist knife. Whoever wanted to enter the city had to reach out first.

    "Half a penny for entering the city." The pacing soldier said in a rough voice, "For those who carry the load, if there is goods on the load, more will be added."

    The team moved forward.

    It was the turn of the old man in front of Jiang Yan to carry the burden. The old man hunched over, took out a cloth bag from his arms, unwrapped it layer by layer, pinched out two shiny copper coins, and handed them over.

    "That's it?" The soldier stopped and glanced at the bundles of dry firewood in the old man's load. "You have no idea how much your firewood can be sold for in the city?"

    "Master Jun..." the old man bent his waist a little more, "This firewood is for Mr. Wang's family in the city. The price has been negotiated long ago, and the little old man can earn some money..."

    "Master Wang?" the soldier sneered, "Which Master Wang, ah? Why don't I recognize it?" He picked at the bundle of firewood with his scabbard, "I think you are a smuggler. Smuggler, take it."

    The old man was anxious: "Master! Master, you can't! This is going to be deducted. This little old man's trip is in vain. I can't explain it when I get back -"

    "Get out of the way." The soldier pushed impatiently.

    The old man staggered, his burden was crooked, and the bundles of firewood were scattered on the ground. He rushed over to pick it up, but the soldier stepped on a bundle and said slowly, "If you want to take it away, fine. Just keep the cloth bag in your arms."

    Jiang Yan stood behind and watched.

    The familiar yet cold thing in his heart slowly surged up.

    There is no difference between Shenjia Village, the manager, and Jiang Goucheng. He changed his body and changed his place, but his methods of bullying were exactly the same. The strong bully the weak; the weak bully the weaker. The world in this world is fundamentally the same bad, from the village to the city.

    No one in line said a word.

    A woman holding a child lowered her head, a man driving a donkey turned his face away, and several refugees stared at their toes with their necks hunched. Everyone saw it, no one looked at it.

    Jiang Yan also lowered his head.

    It's not that he doesn't want to talk. He knew that any word he said now might get him involved. A runaway slave, no money, all injured - he was worse than the old man.

    The old man finally left the cloth bag behind, picked up a few scattered bundles of firewood, carried the mostly empty load, and entered the city without saying a word. When he walked past Jiang Yan, Jiang Yan saw that his eyes were red, but he didn't shed any tears - maybe he had experienced this kind of thing so much that his tears had dried up long ago.

    It's Jiang Yan's turn.
